standard.title: Identify source context and purpose
standard.description: identify the origin, content, context and purpose of primary and secondary sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students identify the origin, content, context and purpose of primary and secondary sources (AC9HH7S03). They can respond to basic origin questions (who, when, why). They have not yet used internal source clues to infer provenance, addressed the difficulty of identifying origin and purpose for ambiguous sources, or analysed how uncertainty about origin affects usefulness.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify the origin, content, context and purpose of primary and secondary sources — responding to who, when, why and what questions, using internal clues to infer provenance, and discussing the difficulties that arise when origin and purpose are uncertain or contested.

nodes.label: Origin, content and purpose questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can systematically apply the four source analysis questions — Who made this? When? Why? What does it show about the past? — to a range of source types including photographs, artefacts, stories and buildings.
nodes.minimum_width: Application of all four questions to at least two different source types with substantive answers (not just labelling).
nodes.typical_width: Systematic four-question analysis applied to the range of source types used in the inquiry — written sources, visual sources, material culture (artefacts, buildings, sites). Understanding that purpose is not always obvious and may require inference from content and context.
wider: Apply the four questions to a source for which one or more answers are uncertain — e.g. an illuminated manuscript of unknown authorship — to practise reasoning about provenance from internal evidence
Compare four-question analyses of two sources covering the same event (e.g. a medieval chronicle and a contemporary artwork) to examine how different origins and purposes produce different content
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic four-question source analysis is the foundation of all subsequent source work. Students who cannot reliably apply all four questions — particularly purpose, which requires inference — cannot assess accuracy and usefulness in S04 or identify perspective in S06.

response_modes.reason: The four-question framework requires reliable, consistent application across varied source types. Students need repeated practice with different source types before they apply the framework accurately and without prompting.

success_criteria: Answers all four source analysis questions (who, when, why, what) for at least two different source types
Explains the purpose of a source through inference rather than just stating the obvious or obvious absence of information

nodes.label: Using internal clues to infer provenance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use clues within a source — including where it was found, materials used, condition, and decorative features — to identify where it was made or who made it.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of using internal source clues to infer origin or maker, with explanation of the reasoning.
nodes.typical_width: Use of physical or contextual clues in artefacts, buildings and visual sources to infer provenance. Examples: using materials, construction techniques and decorative features to identify the period and culture of an artefact; using the location and condition of a source to infer how it was used; connecting the style of illuminated manuscripts to monastic scriptoria.
wider: Examine Viking craft — weapons, armour, longboats — and use design features (keel shape, materials, decorative motifs) to infer when and where items were made, and what they reveal about the society's values and capabilities

Apply provenance inference to Polynesian artefacts such as Lapita pottery from Vanuatu — using clay composition, decoration and find site to make inferences about the movements and contacts of Polynesian peoples

response_modes.reason: Provenance inference from internal clues is a form of detective reasoning that students find unfamiliar. Scaffold the logic explicitly: what does this clue tell us, what does it not tell us, and what else would we need to know to be more confident?

success_criteria: Identifies at least two internal clues in a source and explains what each suggests about the source's origin or maker
Explains the reasoning behind the provenance inference — what the clues suggest and how confident the inference is

nodes.label: Difficulty of identifying origin and purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the difficulty of identifying the origin and purpose of some sources, and explain how this uncertainty affects the source's usefulness in a historical inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of a source where origin or purpose is difficult to determine, with an explanation of how this affects its usefulness.
nodes.typical_width: Cases where origin and purpose are uncertain or contested: anonymous manuscripts, oral traditions committed to writing long after the events they describe, artefacts without context, sites of unknown function. The specific case of Icelandic sagas — oral traditions later written down — as sources whose origin is ambiguous and whose purpose blends history and literature.
wider: Examine how the difficulty of identifying the origin and purpose of Polynesian oral traditions affects their use as historical evidence — and how historians address this by cross-referencing with archaeological evidence

Discuss the monastic scribes' preservation of ancient texts — medieval manuscripts of Greek, Roman and Arab literary works — as sources whose purpose (preservation vs commentary vs distortion) affects how they should be used

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the four-question framework (Node 1) and provenance inference (Node 2) into a higher-order analysis: what happens when those tools cannot resolve uncertainty? Invest in helping students see incomplete provenance as a feature of historical work, not just a gap.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one source where origin or purpose is genuinely uncertain and explains why
Explains how this uncertainty affects what the source can and cannot be used to argue in a historical inquiry
